text.p: Northern Ireland's key Protestant politician, David Trimble, held inconclusive talks with British Prime Minister Tony Blair on the surrender of IRA arms, an issue which has haunted year-long Anglo-Irish peace talks.
Trimble, leader of the Ulster Unionist Party, emerged from the discussions in London and said: "There are some possibilities of progress...but the matter is not yet clear".

He and fellow unionists, which want Northern Ireland to remain under British rule, are angry that Sinn Fein, the political wing of the Irish Republican Army, will be admitted to the talks because the IRA called a truce at the weekend in its 28-year-old campaign of violence to end British rule of Northern Ireland.
Trimble wants the IRA and other guerrilla groups to agree to hand over weapons and bomb-making equipment at the start of talks to end a conflict in which about 3,200 people have died.

Britain's Northern Ireland secretary, Mo Mowlam, who was with Blair at the talks, said Trimble had not threatened to walk out of the peace negotiations in protest against British proposals to sideline the so-called "decommissioning" of IRA arms.

"There is no indication that the UUP were going to walk from the talks which is very useful because, after the ceasefire, what is important to so many people in Northern Ireland is that we do manage to move the talks process forward," she told reporters.
Trimble plans more discussions with British officials ahead of a vote on Britain's "decommissioning" plans on Wednesday at the talks in Belfast co-sponsored by Britain and Ireland.
But a Trimble ally, the U.K. Unionist party, announced that it was pulling out of the talks in protest at what its leader, Robert McCartney, called "terror appeasement" by Britain.

He made the announcement at Belfast's Stormont buildings moments after a Sinn Fein delegation led by Gerry Kelly, a man once convicted of IRA bombing activities, arrived to occupy offices to take part in the talks.

It was the first time Sinn Fein had been allowed to enter the buildings, the former seat of a Northern Irish legislature. The Irish republican party was banned from the talks until the IRA ceasefire and will be permitted to take part in negotiations in six weeks if Britain deems the truce to be genuine.

McCartney said his party, one of three unionist groups committed to British rule of the province, would take no further part in the negotiations except to vote against Britiain's plan to "decommission" arms at the session on Wednesday.
A second unionist group, the Democratic Unionist Party of Ian Paisley, is also threatening to walk out of the talks.

Under British proposals the Irish Republican Army and other guerrilla groups will not have to surrender weapons to gain representation at the talks but must discuss the issue in a sub-committee alongside political negotiations.

Trimble, in his first public comment on the IRA truce, was sharply critical of the government's Northern Ireland office for proposing that Sinn Fein be allowed to take part in negotiations before the IRA hands over a single weapon.
"We are dealing with duplicity from the Northern Ireland office on a massive scale," Trimble told BBC Radio Ulster.
Mitchel McLaughlin, Sinn Fein's chairman, said of Trimble's position:"It is an incredible decision to adopt that the peace process is over because the IRA has called a cessation."

He played down concerns that all three unionist parties might boycott the talks, which would rob them of the consensus required by ground rules to negotiate any settlement between unionists and Irish nationalists.
"I believe those who walk out of the talks will return. The door should be left open so that that can happen," he told reporters when he arrived at Stormont to inspect the offices.
Trimble said the IRA had called the truce because Sinn Fein had been given to understand by Britain that it would not have to secure the handover of any IRA arms during the talks.
"They (Sinn Fein) interpret is as a guarantee that they don't have to carry out any decommissioning at all," he said.
McLaughlin said his understanding was that decommissioning would be part of a final settlement.
"Sinn Fein's view is that we will have decommissioning as part of a comprehensive negotiated agreement," McLaughlin said.
British officials allowed the Sinn Fein delegation to enter the premises where the year-long negotiations have faltered for 13 months over the decommissioning issue.

Delegation leader Kelly, who was jailed for bombing London's Old Bailey court complex in 1972, said he and his aides had come to occupy their offices after the IRA ceasefire and hoped to hold preliminary talks with other parties to the negotiations.
